lesson.title: CI pipeline design: stages, artifacts and caching
lesson.why: A CI pipeline is a team's most-used feedback loop. Good design fails fast on cheap checks, runs expensive work only when it is needed, and ships exactly the build that was tested. Interviewers probe it because slow, flaky or leaky pipelines cost every engineer time daily, and a careless cache or artifact can leak data or deploy something nobody tested.
lesson.what: In GitHub Actions a workflow contains jobs. Every job gets a fresh runner, and jobs run in parallel unless `needs:` orders them, which is how you build stages. Files never flow between jobs by themselves: **artifacts** carry build outputs to later jobs or keep them after the run, while the **dependency cache** speeds up repeated downloads across runs. GitHub's docs are explicit that the two are not interchangeable.

concepts.name: Stages are a dependency graph
concepts.body: Jobs start in parallel; `needs: [lint, test]` makes a job wait for others to succeed, so your stages are really a graph. Put cheap, high-signal checks (lint, unit tests) first and in parallel, and let slow integration or deploy jobs depend on them. `concurrency` with `cancel-in-progress: true` cancels a superseded run on the same branch, and `timeout-minutes` stops a hung job from burning runner time. Set a default `permissions: contents: read` and grant more only to the job that needs it.

concepts.name: Artifacts: build once, promote the same output
concepts.body: `actions/upload-artifact` stores files from a job; `actions/download-artifact` fetches them in a later job of the same run (other runs need a token and run ID). Since v4, artifacts are immutable: upload each name once per run, so matrix jobs need unique names such as `dist-${{ matrix.os }}`. `retention-days` can shorten storage but cannot exceed the repository or organization limit. Build once, then test and deploy that same artifact; rebuilding in the deploy job means you ship something you never tested.

concepts.name: Dependency caching: keys, restore-keys and scope
concepts.body: `actions/cache` first looks for an exact `key` match (a cache hit), then a prefix match, then each `restore-keys` prefix in order, taking the most recent match. On a miss, a new cache is saved when the job succeeds; an existing cache is never changed, so derive the key from what matters, for example `${{ runner.os }}-npm-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}`. Runs can restore caches from the current branch, the default branch and, for pull requests, the base branch. Entries unused for 7 days are removed; the default limit is 10 GB per repository. `setup-node` and `setup-python` can manage the cache for you.

concepts.name: Cache security and correctness
concepts.body: A cache is an optimisation, never a source of truth: the job must still pass on a cold miss. Never write secrets or credentials into a cached path, because anyone who can open a pull request can read base-branch caches. Low-trust triggers such as `pull_request_target`, `issue_comment` and `workflow_run` get read-only access to the default branch's cache scope to prevent cache poisoning; use `actions/cache/restore` or `cache-mode: read` there, and let a trusted `push` workflow keep the cache warm.

e2e: A push or pull request matches the workflow's top-level `on:` triggers.
`concurrency` cancels an older in-progress run for the same branch.
Lint and unit-test jobs start in parallel on fresh runners and restore the dependency cache.
On a cache miss, dependencies install from the registry; the cache is saved when the job succeeds.
The build job (`needs: [lint, test]`) produces `dist/` and uploads it as an artifact with a unique name.
Integration tests download that exact artifact and test it.
A deploy job gated by an environment downloads the same artifact and releases it without rebuilding.
Artifacts expire after their retention period; caches unused for 7 days are evicted.

tasks.name: Redesign a slow single-job pipeline
tasks.goal: Turn one long job into a staged graph that fails fast.
steps: Start from a single job that runs, in order: install, lint, unit tests, build, integration tests, deploy.
Split it into jobs `lint`, `test`, `build`, `integration`, `deploy` and write each job's `needs:`.
Mark which jobs can run in parallel and which is the slowest path.
Add a top-level `concurrency` group with `cancel-in-progress: true`, `timeout-minutes` per job and `permissions: contents: read`.
Write one sentence: which failure now reports fastest, and why.

tasks.name: Predict cache hits and misses
tasks.goal: Reason precisely about cache keys, restore-keys and branch scope.
steps:
Write this step for a Node project:
```yaml
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
```
Now write the equivalent explicit `actions/cache` key using `runner.os` and `hashFiles('**/package-lock.json')`, plus one `restore-keys` prefix.
Predict hit, partial restore or miss: (a) re-run with an unchanged lockfile; (b) lockfile changed; (c) a new branch created from main; (d) a pull request from a fork.
Explain why a partial restore is followed by a fresh install and a new cache entry.

tasks.name: Build once, verify the same artifact
tasks.goal: Prove the later job tests exactly the bytes the build produced.
steps:
In a public GitHub repository (standard GitHub-hosted runners are free there), add `.github/workflows/build-once.yml`:
```yaml
name: build-once
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
permissions:
  contents: read
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: |
          mkdir -p dist
          echo "built from ${{ github.sha }}" > dist/app.txt
          sha256sum dist/app.txt > dist.sha256
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: dist
          path: |
            dist
            dist.sha256
          retention-days: 3
  verify:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          name: dist
      - run: sha256sum --check dist.sha256
```
Push, open the run and confirm `verify` prints `dist/app.txt: OK`.
Change the verify job to rebuild the file instead of downloading it, and explain why the check would no longer prove anything.
Delete the workflow file or the test repository when done; the artifact expires after 3 days.

tasks.name: Review a flawed pipeline
tasks.goal: Spot design defects an interviewer would expect you to catch.
steps: The deploy job runs `npm run build` again instead of downloading the tested artifact.
Three matrix jobs each upload an artifact named `report`.
The cache key is the static string `deps`, and a step writes an npm token into `~/.npm`, the cached path.
No job has `timeout-minutes`, and every job has write permissions.
For each item, state the failure it causes and the one-line fix.

key_terms: Job — a set of steps that runs on one fresh runner; jobs run in parallel unless ordered by `needs`.
`needs` — makes a job wait for other jobs to succeed; how stages are expressed.
Artifact — files uploaded from a job, downloadable by later jobs or after the run until retention ends.
Dependency cache — reusable files (such as package downloads) restored by key across workflow runs.
Cache key / restore-keys — exact match first, then ordered prefix fallbacks; the newest match wins.
`concurrency` — groups runs so a newer run can cancel or queue behind an older one.
Cache poisoning — writing a malicious cache that a more privileged workflow later restores.
lesson.safety: Exercises 1, 2 and 4 are paper exercises. Exercise 3 uses a public GitHub repository, where standard GitHub-hosted runners are free; in a private repository it consumes your included minutes. Use synthetic files only and never put tokens in artifacts, caches or logs.
cleanup: Delete the practice workflow file or the throwaway repository.
Optionally delete the run's artifact from the run page; otherwise it expires after the 3-day retention.
lesson.interview_question: Your team's pull-request pipeline takes 25 minutes, fails randomly about once a day, and the deploy job rebuilds the app before shipping it. Walk me through how you would redesign it, and how you would prove the change helped.
interview_points: Measure first: per-job duration and failure rate from run history.
Stage as a graph: cheap parallel checks first, `needs` for slow jobs, cancel superseded runs.
Cache keyed on the lockfile, with a job that still passes on a cold miss.
Build once and promote the same artifact; add a checksum or provenance check.
Quarantine and fix flaky tests instead of adding blind retries.
lesson.reviewed_at: 2026-09-28 (checked against the official docs listed below)

delivery/ci-pipeline-design-stages-artif.core:
**Core idea:** a pipeline is a graph of jobs, not a script.
- Jobs run in parallel on fresh runners; `needs:` creates stages. Put lint and unit tests first so the cheapest failure reports first.
- **Artifacts** move build output between jobs in a run. They are immutable per name since v4, so each uploader needs a unique name. Build once; test and deploy that same artifact.
- **Caches** speed up dependency installs across runs. Exact `key` hit first, then ordered `restore-keys` prefixes. Key on the lockfile hash, e.g. `hashFiles('**/package-lock.json')`. A cache can never be edited, only replaced by a new key.
- Caches are readable by anyone who can open a pull request, so never cache secrets. Low-trust triggers get read-only access to the default branch's cache.
- Guard rails: `concurrency` + `cancel-in-progress`, `timeout-minutes`, and `permissions: contents: read` by default.

**Artifact vs cache in one line:** artifacts are outputs you keep or pass on; caches are inputs you would rather not download again.

storyboard.title: CI pipeline: stages, cache and one artifact
storyboard.objective: Cheap checks run first, in parallel, on fresh runners.

scenes.title: Fail fast in parallel
scenes.caption: Cheap checks run first, in parallel, on fresh runners.
scenes.narration: A push starts lint and unit tests in parallel. Each job gets a fresh runner, so nothing is shared unless you pass it on deliberately. The cheapest failure reports first.

scenes.title: Restore the dependency cache
scenes.caption: An exact key hit restores packages; a miss installs and saves a new entry.
scenes.narration: The job restores dependencies keyed on the lockfile hash. On an exact hit it skips the download. On a miss it installs normally and saves a new cache when the job succeeds.

scenes.title: Build once
scenes.caption: The build waits for the checks, then uploads one immutable artifact.
scenes.narration: The build job needs lint and tests to pass. It produces the output once and uploads it as an artifact with a unique name. Since version four, that artifact cannot be overwritten.

scenes.title: Promote the tested bytes
scenes.caption: Later jobs download the same artifact instead of rebuilding.
scenes.narration: Integration tests and the deploy job download that same artifact. Rebuilding in the deploy job would ship something that was never tested. A checksum proves the bytes match.

lesson.title: GitHub Actions security: permissions, OIDC, secrets and runners
lesson.why: A CI system holds the keys to production. Most real Actions incidents come from a few patterns: over-privileged tokens, long-lived cloud keys stored as secrets, untrusted pull request code running with secrets, and mutable third-party actions. Knowing the exact rules is what separates 'I use GitHub Actions' from 'I can secure a delivery pipeline'.
lesson.what: Each job gets an automatic `GITHUB_TOKEN` whose access you set with `permissions:`. Instead of storing cloud keys, a job can request a short-lived OpenID Connect (OIDC) token that a cloud provider exchanges for temporary credentials. Secrets are encrypted values with strict rules about where they are available, and runners are the machines that execute your jobs.

concepts.name: GITHUB_TOKEN and permissions
concepts.body: Before each job, GitHub creates an installation token limited to the repository; it expires when the job finishes or reaches its maximum lifetime. If you specify any permission, every permission you do not list becomes `none`; `permissions: {}` removes all. Set `contents: read` at the top and grant writes such as `pull-requests: write` only on the job that needs them. Events created with `GITHUB_TOKEN` do not start new workflow runs (except manual dispatch events).

concepts.name: OIDC: short-lived cloud credentials
concepts.body: `permissions: id-token: write` lets a job request a signed JWT; it grants no write access to repository content. For AWS, the IAM OIDC provider is `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com` with audience `sts.amazonaws.com` for the official action. The role's trust policy must check `aud` and `sub`, for example `repo:OWNER/REPO:ref:refs/heads/main`. When a job uses an environment, `sub` becomes `repo:OWNER/REPO:environment:prod`. Avoid broad wildcards in `sub`.

concepts.name: Secrets and untrusted input
concepts.body: Except for `GITHUB_TOKEN`, secrets are not passed to workflows triggered from forks or by Dependabot, and not automatically to reusable workflows. Redaction relies on exact matches, so never store structured data such as a JSON blob as one secret; use `::add-mask::` for derived values. Put deployment secrets behind an environment with required reviewers. Pass untrusted values such as a pull request title into scripts through `env:` variables, never inline `${{ }}` in `run:`.

concepts.name: Runners and supply chain
concepts.body: GitHub-hosted runners are fresh, isolated VMs for each job. Self-hosted runners give no such guarantee and, per GitHub, should almost never be used for public repositories. Pinning a third-party action to a full-length commit SHA is the only way to use it as an immutable release. `pull_request_target` runs with the base repository's token, secrets and cache access, so executing fork code there is a 'pwn request'. Since June 2026 actions/checkout refuses to fetch a fork pull request's head or merge commit in that context by default, but fetching it another way (`git`, `gh`) is still unsafe.

e2e: A push to main or a manual dispatch starts the deploy workflow.
The job declares `permissions: contents: read` and `id-token: write`, and optionally an environment with reviewers.
The runner requests an OIDC JWT from GitHub with audience `sts.amazonaws.com`.
configure-aws-credentials calls `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` with that JWT.
AWS checks the signature, issuer, `aud` and `sub` against the role's trust policy.
STS returns temporary credentials for the role; no long-lived key exists anywhere.
Later steps call AWS with those credentials and only the role's permissions.
The credentials and the job's GITHUB_TOKEN expire; the hosted runner VM is discarded.

tasks.name: Tighten a workflow's permissions
steps: Take any workflow without a `permissions:` block and add `permissions: contents: read` at the top level.
One job comments on pull requests: grant `pull-requests: write` on that job only.
Explain what happens to `issues` and `packages` access once you list any permission.
Explain why `permissions: {}` is the right choice for a job that needs no API access.

tasks.name: Inspect your OIDC claims without a cloud account
tasks.goal: See the exact `sub` and `aud` a cloud trust policy would check.
steps:
In a public practice repository (GitHub-hosted runners are free there), add:
```yaml
name: oidc-claims
on: workflow_dispatch
permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write
jobs:
  claims:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - uses: actions/github-script@v9
        with:
          script: |
            const token = await core.getIDToken('sts.amazonaws.com');
            const claims = JSON.parse(Buffer.from(token.split('.')[1], 'base64url').toString());
            core.info(`sub=${claims.sub}`);
            core.info(`aud=${claims.aud}`);
            core.info(`ref=${claims.ref} environment=${claims.environment ?? 'none'}`);
```
Run it from the Actions tab. The job prints only claims, never the token itself.
Add `environment: practice` to the job, run again and compare how `sub` changed.
Delete the workflow when finished.

tasks.name: Write and test a trust policy on paper
tasks.goal: Limit which workflows can assume a cloud role.
steps: Can a workflow on branch `feature/x` assume the role? A job using `environment: prod`? Explain using the `sub` values you printed.

Rewrite the condition so only jobs in the `prod` environment can assume it. The job that uses the role looks like this:
```yaml
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: prod
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gha-deploy
          aws-region: ap-south-1
      - run: aws sts get-caller-identity
```
Explain what `repo:OWNER/*` in a `StringLike` condition would allow, and why that is risky.

tasks.name: Review a risky workflow
tasks.goal: Find the supply-chain and secret-handling defects.
steps: It runs on `pull_request_target`, checks out the pull request's head commit and runs `npm test` with a deploy secret in `env`.
A step runs `echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"` inline in `run:`.
A third-party action is referenced by a moving major tag, and the job uses a self-hosted runner in a public repository.
Cloud credentials are stored as one JSON blob secret.
For each defect, describe the attack and the fix.

key_terms: GITHUB_TOKEN — per-job installation token scoped to the repository; access set by `permissions:`.
`id-token: write` — lets a job request an OIDC JWT; grants no repository write access.
`sub` claim — identifies repository and ref or environment; the key trust-policy condition.
`aud` claim — intended audience; `sts.amazonaws.com` for the official AWS action.
Environment — deployment target with protection rules and its own secrets.
Commit-SHA pinning — the only immutable way to reference an action.
`pull_request_target` — runs in the base repository context with its secrets; never run fork code.
lesson.safety: Exercises 1, 3 and 4 are paper exercises and exercise 2 needs only a free public GitHub repository. Never print tokens or secrets, even in a practice repository. If you later create a real AWS role, use a sandbox account and a least-privilege permission policy.
cleanup: Delete the practice workflow or repository.
If you created an AWS OIDC provider or role while experimenting, delete them when finished.
lesson.interview_question: Your company stores an AWS access key as a repository secret so GitHub Actions can deploy. Security asks you to remove it. Design the replacement, including exactly what AWS checks and how you stop a feature branch or a fork from deploying to production.
interview_points: OIDC federation: IAM OIDC provider plus a role; `id-token: write` in the job.
Trust policy checks `aud` and an exact `sub`, ideally the prod environment.
Environment with required reviewers, deploying only from main.
Least-privilege role permissions and a top-level `contents: read` default.
Forks get no secrets and cannot mint a matching `sub`; never use pull_request_target to run fork code.

delivery/github-actions-permissions-oidc.core:
**Core idea:** give every job the least access, for the shortest time.
- `permissions:` sets GITHUB_TOKEN access. List any permission and all others become `none`. Default to `contents: read`; add writes per job.
- **OIDC** replaces stored cloud keys. `id-token: write` lets the job request a signed JWT, and AWS STS swaps it for temporary credentials. The trust policy must check `aud` (`sts.amazonaws.com`) and an exact `sub`, e.g. `repo:OWNER/REPO:environment:prod`.
- **Secrets** are not given to fork or Dependabot runs. Don't store a JSON blob as one secret: redaction needs exact matches. Pass untrusted text via `env:`, not inline `${{ }}`.
- **Runners and actions**: hosted runners are fresh VMs. Avoid self-hosted runners on public repos. Pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA, and never run fork code under `pull_request_target`.

Today's exercises need only a free public GitHub repository.

storyboard.title: GitHub Actions OIDC deploy without stored keys
storyboard.objective: The job asks GitHub for a signed JWT for audience sts.amazonaws.com.

scenes.title: Request an identity token
scenes.caption: The job asks GitHub for a signed JWT for audience sts.amazonaws.com.
scenes.narration: The deploy job has permission to request an identity token. GitHub's OIDC provider issues a short-lived signed token whose subject names the repository and branch or environment.

scenes.title: Exchange it with AWS
scenes.caption: The official action calls AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with the token.
scenes.narration: The configure credentials action sends the token to AWS security token service and asks to assume one specific role. No access key is stored in GitHub at any point.

scenes.title: Trust policy decides
scenes.caption: AWS checks issuer, signature, audience and the exact subject claim.
scenes.narration: AWS validates the token and compares the audience and subject with the role's trust policy. A feature branch or fork produces a different subject, so the request is denied.

scenes.title: Temporary, least-privilege access
scenes.caption: Later steps use short-lived credentials limited by the role's policy.
scenes.narration: Security token service returns temporary credentials. Later steps can call only what the role's permission policy allows, and the credentials expire on their own.

lesson.title: GitLab CI pipelines environments and deployment controls
lesson.why: A pipeline graph and a deployment permission model solve different problems. Manual buttons alone do not establish safe production authorization.
lesson.what: Model GitLab stages, needs dependencies, artifacts, environments, and serialized deployment controls.

concepts.name: Pipeline graph
concepts.body: Stages provide default ordering while needs can form a more direct dependency graph. Jobs should depend on required evidence rather than arbitrary stage names. Rules determine whether jobs exist for a pipeline source, so test branch and merge-request cases explicitly.

concepts.name: Artifacts and dependencies
concepts.body: Artifacts carry tested outputs between jobs; caches accelerate reusable work. When using needs, declare appropriate artifact relationships rather than assuming every earlier artifact arrives automatically. Give release artifacts clear identity and retention matching the deployment and recovery window.

concepts.name: Environment authorization
concepts.body: Environments record deployment targets, and protected-environment controls can restrict authorized deployers where supported. A manual job is a pause, not a complete security boundary. Protect credentials and runner access independently, especially when merge-request code can influence scripts.

concepts.name: Deployment serialization
concepts.body: Resource groups serialize jobs sharing a deployment resource so concurrent pipelines do not overwrite the same environment. Serialization does not decide whether an older release should run after a newer one. Add freshness checks, cancellation policy, and compatibility-aware rollback rules.

e2e: Pipeline rules select the intended validation and release jobs.
Tests and build jobs create verified artifacts with explicit dependencies.
An authorized deployment job acquires the environment's serialization resource.
The job deploys the approved artifact and records health and deployment evidence.

tasks.name: Compute graph duration
steps: Lint takes two minutes, tests eight, and packaging three after tests. Deployment requires packaging and lint, so the ideal critical path is eleven minutes before deployment. Moving packaging before its tests complete may shorten elapsed time but changes the evidence dependency and needs explicit justification.

tasks.name: Review job rules
steps: Create a truth table for merge requests, ordinary branch pushes, and protected release tags. Include test jobs in all intended validation cases but production deployment only in the authorized release case. Explain why omitting a rule can silently remove required evidence rather than fail a pipeline.

tasks.name: Model concurrent releases
steps: Pipeline A builds revision one slowly; B builds revision two quickly. Both target production using one resource group. Show that a lock prevents overlap but can still allow A after B unless freshness policy rejects the stale release. Record the expected newest approved version.

tasks.name: Design recovery evidence
steps: For a fictional environment, retain the current and previous artifact digests, deployment identities, and health checks. Separate an approval action from permission to read deployment variables. Describe why an expired artifact can make a rollback button operationally useless despite valid authorization.

key_terms: needs: explicit job dependency relationship.
Environment: named deployment target.
Resource group: deployment concurrency control.
Rules: conditions deciding job inclusion.
lesson.safety: Use paper pipeline graphs; do not trigger pipelines or expose deployment variables.
cleanup: Discard the fictional rules table; no runner or environment configuration changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, an older GitLab pipeline deploys after a newer release. Why did serialization alone not prevent this?
interview_points: Locks prevent concurrency, not stale ordering.
Bind deployment to approved artifact and freshness checks.
Review cancellation and rollback policy separately.

storyboard.title: Serialized deployment still needs freshness checks
storyboard.objective: Prevent an old pipeline from overwriting a newer release.

scenes.title: New release arrives first
scenes.caption: The environment is updated safely.
scenes.narration: The newer pipeline acquires the resource group and deploys revision two.

scenes.title: Old job becomes ready
scenes.caption: A lock does not imply freshness.
scenes.narration: The older pipeline finishes later and could otherwise deploy revision one next.

scenes.title: Reject stale promotion
scenes.caption: Approval and revision must still match.
scenes.narration: A freshness gate rejects the obsolete deployment while preserving the newer healthy release.

delivery/gitlab-ci-pipelines-environment.core: Use explicit job and artifact dependencies, protected deployment authority, resource-group serialization, and freshness gates. A manual job or lock alone is insufficient.

lesson.title: Jenkins pipelines agents credentials and shared libraries
lesson.why: Jenkins flexibility creates powerful execution paths. Pipeline code, agent access, and trusted libraries need clear ownership to avoid turning routine builds into privileged operations.
lesson.what: Design a bounded Jenkins pipeline with isolated agents, scoped credentials, and versioned shared behavior.

concepts.name: Pipeline as code
concepts.body: A Jenkinsfile records build stages and control flow with the source change. Declarative and scripted pipelines differ in structure but both execute code. Timeouts, failure propagation, and explicit artifact identity keep a hung or partially failed build from becoming an ambiguous release.

concepts.name: Agent boundaries
concepts.body: Agents execute jobs and may hold workspace remnants or network access. Controller administration is a separate responsibility and should not become ordinary build execution. Isolate untrusted contributions from privileged agents and avoid giving generic builds access to container-host administration.

concepts.name: Credential scope
concepts.body: Credential bindings provide values to selected steps, but code in those steps can use them. Masking is not access control. Narrow binding duration, avoid interpolation that exposes secrets through process arguments, and separate trusted deployment jobs from untrusted repository scripts.

concepts.name: Shared libraries
concepts.body: Libraries centralize pipeline functions and policies but also concentrate authority. Pin reviewed versions and distinguish trusted libraries from sandboxed code. A library update can affect many repositories, so test compatibility and promote library revisions deliberately rather than silently following a moving branch.

e2e: A reviewed Jenkinsfile selects an appropriately isolated agent.
Validation and build stages produce a traceable artifact without deployment secrets.
A trusted release stage binds only the required credential for its operation.
Post conditions retain evidence and release resources while preserving the actual failure status.

tasks.name: Calculate bounded execution
steps: A test stage has a ten-minute timeout and a deployment stage a five-minute timeout. Sequential execution is bounded near fifteen minutes plus queueing and cleanup, not five minutes. If tests time out, deployment must remain blocked rather than continue because cleanup succeeded.

tasks.name: Map agent authority
steps: Create three fictional labels: untrusted-test, trusted-build, and deploy. Assign no secrets to the first and narrow network access to each. Explain why a label is only routing metadata unless provisioning and permissions actually enforce the intended isolation.

tasks.name: Review a credential scope
steps: A credential wraps checkout, arbitrary tests, and deployment. Move the binding conceptually to the smallest trusted deployment step. Identify shell arguments, archived workspaces, and helper logs as possible disclosure paths even when the console masks the literal secret value.

tasks.name: Plan a library upgrade
steps: A shared library changes its artifact naming contract. Test the new version against two representative repositories, document the migration, and pin consumers to reviewed revisions. Include a compatibility rollback and explain why reverting the library cannot restore an already overwritten external artifact.

key_terms: Jenkinsfile: versioned pipeline definition.
Agent: job execution worker.
Credential binding: scoped credential exposure.
Shared library: reusable pipeline code package.
lesson.safety: Use fictional agents and credentials; do not contact a Jenkins controller or run privileged builds.
cleanup: Discard the routing and timeout tables; no jobs were changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a shared library update breaks dozens of Jenkins releases. How would you contain impact and prevent recurrence?
interview_points: Pin reviewed library revisions and test representative consumers.
Separate library authority from untrusted application code.
Restore compatible versions while checking external side effects.

storyboard.title: Shared pipeline code needs controlled promotion
storyboard.objective: Show the blast radius of moving library versions.

scenes.title: Test a new contract
scenes.caption: Library changes affect callers.
scenes.narration: A representative pipeline exercises the proposed artifact naming behavior.

scenes.title: Detect incompatibility
scenes.caption: Do not update every caller yet.
scenes.narration: The changed output contract breaks a release consumer and blocks broad promotion.

scenes.title: Promote compatible revisions
scenes.caption: Consumers choose reviewed versions.
scenes.narration: A corrected library is rolled out through explicit pinned revisions with recovery evidence.

delivery/jenkins-pipelines-agents-creden.core: Treat pipeline and library code as authority-bearing software. Isolate agents, narrowly bind credentials, preserve failure signals, and promote reviewed shared-library versions.

lesson.title: Build reproducibility dependency pinning and provenance
lesson.why: Knowing the source commit is not enough to reproduce or trust a binary. Toolchains, dependencies, build context, and evidence all affect release integrity.
lesson.what: Distinguish repeatable inputs, byte-identical output, and signed provenance using local hashing and an offline build inventory.

concepts.name: Complete inputs
concepts.body: Pin source, dependency versions and checksums, compiler or runtime version, base images, and build parameters. Floating tags or external downloads can change without a source commit. Lock files record selections but must actually be enforced by the installation command.

concepts.name: Deterministic output
concepts.body: Reproducibility means independent builds with equivalent defined inputs produce the expected identical output. Timestamps, file ordering, locale, and embedded paths can introduce differences. Removing nondeterminism requires understanding the format, not simply ignoring every changed byte.

concepts.name: Provenance evidence
concepts.body: Provenance describes how an artifact was produced, linking its digest to source and build identity. Signatures authenticate the evidence issuer, not the absence of vulnerabilities. Verify trusted builder identity and policy before accepting an attestation from an arbitrary source.

concepts.name: Dependency updates
concepts.body: Pinning reduces surprise but does not keep software secure forever. Use deliberate update workflows, vulnerability triage, and compatibility tests. Keep old artifacts available for operational recovery while avoiding indefinite rollback to versions with unacceptable known risk.

e2e: Resolve and record the complete reviewed build input set.
Build in a controlled environment with nondeterministic sources minimized.
Hash output and attach provenance identifying source and builder.
Verify digest and trusted evidence before promoting the same artifact.

tasks.name: Check byte identity
steps: Run python -c "import hashlib; a=b'release'; b=b'release'; print(hashlib.sha256(a).digest()==hashlib.sha256(b).digest())". Expected output is True. Change b to b'release\n' and expect False; seemingly cosmetic bytes still change artifact identity and require explanation.

tasks.name: Inventory hidden inputs
steps: A build records its Git commit but installs latest dependencies and embeds the current time. Identify both moving inputs and add locked dependency data plus a documented timestamp policy. Explain why rerunning the same commit tomorrow is not yet a reproducibility test.

tasks.name: Evaluate an attestation
steps: A package has a valid signature from an unknown identity. Reject automatic trust until issuer, builder, source revision, and artifact digest match policy. Explain why a correctly signed malicious build remains malicious and why provenance complements rather than replaces testing.

tasks.name: Plan safe updates
steps: A pinned dependency receives a security fix. Propose a dedicated update change, regenerated lock data, compatibility tests, and a new provenance record. Preserve the previous digest for investigation while documenting whether its security risk permits operational rollback.

key_terms: Pinning: fixing a dependency selection.
Reproducibility: equivalent inputs yield identical output.
Provenance: recorded artifact production evidence.
Attestation: authenticated statement about an artifact.
lesson.safety: Hash only supplied synthetic bytes; do not download or execute unverified build artifacts.
cleanup: The comparison writes no files; discard the input inventory.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, two builds from one commit produce different digests despite valid signatures. What would you investigate?
interview_points: Compare dependencies, toolchains, timestamps, and build context.
Verify each signature's trusted builder identity.
Explain differences before accepting either artifact for promotion.

storyboard.title: Same source does not guarantee the same artifact
storyboard.objective: Connect complete inputs with trustworthy build evidence.

scenes.title: Record inputs
scenes.caption: Source is one dependency among several.
scenes.narration: The builder records dependencies and toolchain alongside the source revision.

scenes.title: Find a differing digest
scenes.caption: A hidden input may have changed.
scenes.narration: An embedded timestamp produces different bytes despite an unchanged source commit.

scenes.title: Verify controlled output
scenes.caption: Evidence binds the exact bytes.
scenes.narration: A deterministic build and trusted provenance connect the artifact digest to reviewed inputs.

delivery/build-reproducibility-dependenc.core: Pin all meaningful inputs, investigate nondeterministic output, and verify provenance against trusted builder policy. Signatures do not prove software is safe.

lesson.title: Automated test strategy and flaky-test management
lesson.why: An unreliable test suite trains teams to ignore failures. Good coverage gives fast, attributable evidence while reserving expensive tests for risks they uniquely detect.
lesson.what: Combine unit, integration, contract, and end-to-end tests with disciplined flake investigation and bounded quarantine.

concepts.name: Risk-based layers
concepts.body: Unit tests isolate logic cheaply; integration tests exercise real component boundaries; contract tests verify agreed interfaces; end-to-end tests cover user journeys. More end-to-end tests are not automatically better because slow, broad failures often provide poor fault localization.

concepts.name: Deterministic fixtures
concepts.body: Control time, random seeds, external responses, and test data ownership. Avoid shared mutable accounts and order-dependent setup. Isolation improves parallelism and makes a failing example reproducible without requiring the entire suite to run in a particular sequence.

concepts.name: Flake evidence
concepts.body: A flaky test changes outcome without a relevant product change. Record failure signatures, retry outcomes, environment, and timing. Retrying can collect evidence but must not silently convert every failure into success or obscure a genuine intermittent product defect.

concepts.name: Quarantine governance
concepts.body: Quarantine removes a known unreliable gate temporarily while preserving execution and visibility. Assign an owner, expiry, and coverage replacement if the test protects critical behavior. Track first-attempt failure and escape rates rather than reporting only green results after retries.

e2e: Map product risks to the cheapest test layer that can detect them.
Run isolated fixtures and preserve first-attempt failures with context.
Classify deterministic defects, environment failures, and suspected flakes.
Repair or time-bound quarantine, then verify repeated clean execution and restored coverage.

tasks.name: Calculate retry masking
steps: One hundred tests run; ten fail initially and eight pass on retry. Final failures are two, but first-attempt pass rate is 90 percent, not 98 percent. Record both figures and investigate the eight recoveries rather than calling them proven harmless flakes.

tasks.name: Choose test layers
steps: Assign a tax calculation to unit tests, database transaction behavior to integration tests, response-field compatibility to contract tests, and one checkout journey to end-to-end testing. Explain which real dependency each layer must include and which can be controlled.

tasks.name: Reproduce an order dependency
steps: Test A creates user demo; test B expects no users. Predict B fails only after A when both share one database. Give each test isolated data or transactional cleanup, then reverse the order and run concurrently to verify the dependency has disappeared.

tasks.name: Write quarantine criteria
steps: A browser test times out intermittently at login. Record its owner, observed signature, expiry date, and a smaller replacement authentication check. Keep running it outside the release gate and require evidence before restoration; do not disable unrelated failing tests under the same label.

key_terms: Contract test: interface compatibility check.
Fixture: controlled test setup and data.
Flake: outcome variation without relevant change.
Quarantine: temporary removal from gating with ownership.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic test outcomes; do not load-test production or reuse real customer accounts.
cleanup: Discard the offline test matrix; no test gates were disabled.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, your suite is green only after automatic retries. How would you restore trust without stopping all delivery indefinitely?
interview_points: Expose first-attempt failure and classify signatures.
Fix isolation and nondeterministic dependencies.
Use owned, expiring quarantine with replacement coverage.

storyboard.title: A retry can hide a failing test contract

scenes.title: Capture failure
scenes.caption: First-attempt quality matters.
scenes.narration: The suite records the failing test and its environment before any retry.

scenes.title: Retry passes
scenes.caption: Success does not explain the failure.
scenes.narration: A passing retry identifies variation but does not prove the product is correct.

scenes.title: Repair the source
scenes.caption: Quarantine has an owner and deadline.
scenes.narration: An owner fixes shared state or bounds quarantine while preserving coverage evidence.

delivery/automated-test-strategy-and-fla.core: Match tests to risks, isolate fixtures, retain first-attempt results, and investigate retries. Quarantine must be owned, visible, temporary, and covered by compensating evidence.

lesson.title: Deployment blue-green canary and rolling strategies
lesson.why: Deployment strategy determines who experiences a defect and how quickly recovery can occur. Traffic, capacity, and data compatibility matter more than the strategy's label.
lesson.what: Compare blue-green cutover, canary exposure, and rolling replacement using explicit capacity and error calculations.

concepts.name: Blue-green environments
concepts.body: Two environments allow a traffic switch between known versions. Keeping the old environment can shorten application rollback, but duplicate capacity costs resources. Shared databases and external side effects still need compatibility; switching traffic does not reverse writes.

concepts.name: Canary exposure
concepts.body: A canary exposes a bounded population to the new version and compares meaningful indicators. Traffic percentage is not always user percentage because sessions, geography, and request patterns differ. Low-volume canaries may need longer observation to reveal rare failures.

concepts.name: Rolling replacement
concepts.body: Rolling updates replace instances gradually while old and new versions coexist. They require spare or temporarily reduced capacity and backward-compatible interactions. Readiness, connection draining, and version-skew support determine whether nominally available instances actually serve users safely.

concepts.name: Decision gates
concepts.body: Predeclare success, pause, and rollback thresholds using user outcomes and diagnostic signals. A rollout controller needs enough observations, not just a green process check. Keep recovery artifacts ready and validate that old code remains compatible with current data.

e2e: Choose exposure and capacity limits based on failure impact.
Start the new version while preserving compatible serving capacity.
Observe comparison signals over a meaningful population and time window.
Increase exposure or recover using the predefined gate and data-safe procedure.

tasks.name: Calculate canary impact
steps: A service receives 10000 requests during observation and routes 5 percent to canary: 500 requests. If canary has twenty errors, its error ratio is 4 percent. Stable has nineteen errors among 9500 requests, or 0.2 percent. The aggregate hides a large version-specific regression.

tasks.name: Compare capacity plans
steps: Ten instances serve normal demand. Full blue-green duplication needs twenty during overlap; a rolling policy adding two at a time peaks at twelve. Discuss whether the cheaper overlap has enough failure headroom and whether rollback requires retained old capacity.

tasks.name: Design session routing
steps: A canary uses sticky sessions for ten percent of users. Explain why a few heavy users may generate much more than ten percent of requests. Record both user and request exposure, and avoid treating inconsistent routing as proof that the load balancer is broken.

tasks.name: Choose a recovery gate
steps: Set a hypothetical pause threshold for version-specific errors and require enough samples before promotion. Then assume the new version changed a database schema. Verify old-version compatibility before traffic reversal and use forward repair if reversing code would corrupt or reject current data.

key_terms: Blue-green: switching between parallel environments.
Canary: bounded new-version exposure.
Rolling update: gradual instance replacement.
Gate: predefined rollout decision condition.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic traffic counts; do not shift real traffic or create duplicate paid environments.
cleanup: Discard the capacity and error tables; no release was started.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, aggregate errors look healthy while canary users report failures. How would you decide whether to continue rollout?
interview_points: Compare version-specific rates and meaningful sample counts.
Check routing population and session bias.
Pause exposure and verify data-compatible recovery.

storyboard.title: Aggregate health can hide a bad canary
storyboard.objective: Compare new-version outcomes before increasing exposure.

scenes.title: Bound exposure
scenes.caption: Most traffic stays stable.
scenes.narration: The router sends a small measured request population to the new version.

scenes.title: Canary errors rise
scenes.caption: Aggregate metrics dilute the signal.
scenes.narration: Version-specific error rates reveal a regression hidden by the larger stable population.

scenes.title: Stop expansion
scenes.caption: Recover before broader exposure.
scenes.narration: The rollout pauses and restores stable routing after checking data compatibility.

delivery/deployment-blue-green-canary-an.core: Choose rollout strategy by exposure, capacity, and compatibility. Evaluate version-specific outcomes, predeclare gates, and remember traffic rollback does not undo data changes.

lesson.title: Database migrations backward compatibility and rollout
lesson.why: Application rollback fails when database changes remove assumptions the previous version needs. Schema evolution should preserve a deliberate compatibility window.
lesson.what: Use expand, backfill, switch, and contract phases to change a data model while old and new application instances coexist.

concepts.name: Expand first
concepts.body: Add compatible schema elements before requiring them in application code. New nullable columns or separate structures can preserve old readers, but defaults, locks, and rewrite behavior depend on the database and version. Test operational impact on representative data size.

concepts.name: Backfill safely
concepts.body: Historical data needs bounded migration with checkpoints, retries, and idempotent updates. Large unbounded transactions can create lock contention and replication lag. Throttle by measured database health and verify completeness using counts and semantic checks, not only job success.

concepts.name: Dual-version operation
concepts.body: During rolling deployment, old and new code may read and write concurrently. Define the source of truth and how dual writes stay consistent. A partially successful pair of writes needs reconciliation; calling both APIs does not create atomicity automatically.

concepts.name: Contract last
concepts.body: Remove obsolete fields only after every relevant reader and writer has migrated and the rollback window is intentionally closed. Include background jobs, exports, and analytics consumers. Destructive cleanup may require restore rather than ordinary code rollback if assumptions prove wrong.

e2e: Expand schema while preserving old application behavior.
Backfill historical records in observable, restartable batches.
Switch compatible readers and writers while checking reconciliation evidence.
Retire old consumers and contract the schema only after explicit approval.

tasks.name: Calculate backfill duration
steps: A table has 120000 rows and batches process 1000 rows every two seconds. It needs 120 batches and at least 240 seconds before retries, throttling, and validation. If one batch retries, its idempotent update must not duplicate the logical data transformation.

tasks.name: Build a compatibility matrix
steps: Old code reads full_name; new code reads display_name. Add display_name without dropping full_name, then test old and new code against the expanded schema. Mark old code plus a schema lacking full_name as incompatible and prevent that destructive combination during the rollback window.

tasks.name: Diagnose inconsistent writes
tasks.goal: Define a repairable source of truth.
steps: A request updates full_name successfully but the display_name write fails. Choose an authoritative value and a reconciliation process rather than assuming both fields agree. Explain when a database transaction can make the pair atomic and when cross-system writes need another design.

tasks.name: Approve final contraction
steps: Inventory API instances, scheduled reports, ETL jobs, and dashboards using the old field. Require observation over their actual execution cycles and a tested recovery plan before removal. A quiet five-minute window cannot prove that a monthly report no longer depends on the column.

key_terms: Expand-contract: compatibility-preserving migration sequence.
Backfill: populating historical records.
Checkpoint: durable migration progress marker.
Dual write: updating old and new representations.
lesson.safety: Use fictional records; never run schema changes, mass updates, or drop commands against a real database.
cleanup: Discard the migration matrix; no database objects were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a new release renamed a column and rollback now fails. How would you redesign the migration sequence?
interview_points: Expand before switching consumers and contract last.
Backfill idempotently with bounded load and checks.
Include hidden readers and preserve a defined rollback window.

storyboard.title: Keep both schemas during the compatibility window
storyboard.objective: Show why destructive cleanup comes last.

scenes.title: Expand compatibly
scenes.caption: Old readers continue working.
scenes.narration: The expanded schema preserves the old field while introducing the new representation.

scenes.title: Premature removal breaks rollback
scenes.caption: Old consumers still exist.
scenes.narration: Dropping the old field before migration completes makes the previous application incompatible.

scenes.title: Migrate and then contract
scenes.caption: Evidence closes the old contract.
scenes.narration: After backfill and all reader transitions are verified, obsolete schema can be retired deliberately.

delivery/database-migrations-backward-co.core: Expand, backfill, switch, then contract. Preserve compatibility across mixed application versions, bound migration load, and verify every consumer before destructive cleanup.

lesson.title: Feature flags progressive delivery and rollback
lesson.why: Separating deployment from exposure can reduce release risk, but flags add runtime dependencies and configuration states that require testing and ownership.
lesson.what: Design deterministic cohorts, safe defaults, operational kill switches, and flag retirement with an offline rollout calculation.

concepts.name: Exposure control
concepts.body: A feature flag selects behavior without necessarily redeploying code. It can support staged enablement or emergency disablement. The old path must remain functional while rollback is promised; a disabled flag cannot restore code or data that has already been removed.

concepts.name: Stable cohorts
concepts.body: Deterministic assignment keeps users in consistent treatment groups and improves comparison. Random selection on every request causes unstable experience and confounds results. Percentage of identities differs from percentage of requests when activity levels vary across users.

concepts.name: Failure defaults
concepts.body: Flag evaluation may depend on cached configuration or a remote service. Define behavior during timeout, stale data, or missing flags. Security and authorization checks must not become fail-open experimental toggles; separate entitlement enforcement from optional product exposure.

concepts.name: Lifecycle ownership
concepts.body: Every temporary flag needs an owner, purpose, expiry, and removal plan. Interacting flags multiply possible states and testing burden. Operational kill switches may be long-lived, but they still require exercises, monitoring, and clear authority to change them.

e2e: Deploy code with a safe default and functioning previous path.
Assign a stable bounded cohort and measure version-specific outcomes.
Increase exposure or disable the feature according to predefined gates.
Remove obsolete branches and configuration after the rollback promise expires.

tasks.name: Calculate cohort selection
steps: Assign fictional user IDs 0 through 99 to buckets equal to ID modulo 100. Enable buckets below ten: exactly ten of the hundred IDs qualify. Raising the threshold to twenty preserves those ten and adds ten more; this toy model illustrates stable assignment, not secure anonymization.

tasks.name: Define outage behavior
steps: A recommendation flag service times out. Decide whether cached last-known configuration or a disabled optional feature is appropriate. Contrast that with an authorization decision, which must continue enforcing access independently rather than granting permission because flag data is unavailable.

tasks.name: Diagnose rollback failure
steps: A flagged feature writes a new record format and the old path cannot read it. Explain why switching the flag off is not sufficient recovery. Add compatible readers or a forward-repair plan before enabling more users, and document how already-written records are handled.

tasks.name: Reduce flag debt
steps: Four independent Boolean flags produce 2^4=16 possible combinations. Identify mutually exclusive or obsolete flags, choose critical interaction tests, and assign retirement owners. Explain why testing only all-on and all-off misses fourteen combinations in the full model.

key_terms: Flag: runtime behavior selector.
Cohort: stable exposure population.
Kill switch: operational feature-disable control.
Flag debt: accumulated obsolete branching complexity.
lesson.safety: Use fictional users; do not change live flags or use personal identifiers in experiments.
cleanup: Discard the bucket table; no flag-service configuration changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, disabling a feature flag does not recover affected users. Which assumptions would you challenge?
interview_points: Check data compatibility and retained old behavior.
Inspect cached configuration and cohort propagation.
Separate exposure rollback from irreversible side effects.

storyboard.title: A flag controls exposure, not past side effects
storyboard.objective: Show safe enablement and compatible rollback.

scenes.title: Expose a small cohort
scenes.caption: Assignment stays stable.
scenes.narration: The flag enables the new behavior for a bounded consistent population.

scenes.title: New writes break old reads
scenes.caption: Disabling cannot undo data changes.
scenes.narration: An incompatible record format makes the previous path unsafe despite the flag switch.

scenes.title: Restore compatibility
scenes.caption: Recovery needs a working old contract.
scenes.narration: Compatible readers or repaired data make disabling exposure an effective recovery action.

delivery/feature-flags-progressive-deliv.core: Flags decouple deployment and exposure but not data reversibility. Use stable cohorts, explicit outage defaults, independent authorization, and owned retirement plans.
objectives: Design flag failure and retirement policy

lesson.title: Release approvals change management and audit trails
lesson.why: An approval is meaningful only when it identifies what was reviewed and who may execute it. Vague approvals create confidence without control.
lesson.what: Design evidence-bound release gates, emergency exceptions, and durable audit records that support accountability without unnecessary delay.

concepts.name: Approval binding
concepts.body: Bind approval to source revision, artifact digest, target environment, planned actions, and relevant test evidence. If those inputs change, the approval may no longer apply. A green button on an unrelated build is not authorization for new bytes.

concepts.name: Separation of duties
concepts.body: Distinct proposal and approval authority can reduce unchecked high-impact changes. Apply proportional controls based on risk rather than requiring identical ceremony for every edit. Automated low-risk checks can reduce waiting while preserving independent review for destructive or sensitive operations.

concepts.name: Emergency paths
concepts.body: Emergency changes need a documented reason, bounded authority, incident linkage, and retrospective review. Break-glass access should be time-limited and logged. An emergency process is not a permanent alternate route around tests, evidence, or access reviews.

concepts.name: Audit quality
concepts.body: Useful audit records connect actor, time, target, artifact, decision, execution outcome, and recovery actions. Restrict tampering and retention access while avoiding secrets or unnecessary personal data. Logs prove recorded events, not automatically the correctness of the deployed application.

e2e: Collect release evidence and classify operational risk.
An authorized reviewer approves the exact target and change identity.
A scoped executor deploys only the approved artifact and records results.
Health verification closes the change or invokes documented recovery and follow-up.

tasks.name: Calculate gate freshness
steps: Approval covers artifact digest A and configuration revision 7. A later rebuild produces digest B while revision remains 7. The matching fields are one of two identity inputs; expected decision is reapproval, not fifty-percent confidence or automatic reuse of the old approval.

tasks.name: Design an evidence record
steps: For a fictional release, record source commit, artifact digest, environment, test summary, approver identity, execution identity, start time, and health outcome. Keep credential values out. Explain how an investigator would connect a user-visible incident to this exact release.

tasks.name: Classify change risk
steps: Compare a documentation edit, a stateless replica increase, and a database deletion. Choose automated validation, operational review, or explicit recovery evidence according to impact. Explain why equal approval ceremony can waste attention while still missing the truly irreversible change.

tasks.name: Plan emergency closure
steps: A critical outage needs a hotfix before the ordinary window. Define temporary authorization, incident reference, exact artifact, rollback conditions, and a next-day review owner. Require the durable source and normal controls to catch up after recovery rather than leaving an undocumented production-only patch.

key_terms: Approval: authorization for identified change.
Audit trail: linked durable execution evidence.
Break-glass: exceptional bounded access path.
Change risk: expected impact and reversibility.
lesson.safety: Use fictional identities and artifacts; do not grant permissions or approve actual releases.
cleanup: Discard the sample record; no real audit data was copied.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, production runs a rebuilt artifact under yesterday's approval. What control failed and how would you repair it?
interview_points: Bind approvals to exact artifact and configuration identity.
Invalidate approval when relevant inputs change.
Retain linked execution evidence and proportionate emergency procedures.

storyboard.title: Approval follows artifact identity
storyboard.objective: Prevent stale evidence from authorizing different bytes.

scenes.title: Review exact inputs
scenes.caption: Approval has a defined subject.
scenes.narration: The reviewer authorizes artifact A and its intended environment.

scenes.title: Rebuild changes identity
scenes.caption: Artifact B is not covered.
scenes.narration: The executor detects a different digest and blocks deployment under stale approval.

scenes.title: Revalidate changed bytes
scenes.caption: New identity needs matching evidence.
scenes.narration: Fresh test evidence and approval permit execution of the deliberately selected artifact.

delivery/release-approvals-change-manage.core: Approvals bind exact source, artifact, configuration, and target. Use proportional controls, bounded emergency access, and linked tamper-resistant audit evidence without secrets.
